q-99056:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}-2}) \\  & =\frac{(2x-3)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)-(2x-3)\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)^{′}}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)-(2x-3)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-4+6x-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2{x}^{2}-6x+4}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2{x}^{2}-6x+4}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-6x+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=1$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist at $x=\pm \sqrt{2}.$ But these points do not lie in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=2.$

q-99053:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+6}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)-(2x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)-(2x+1)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+12-4{x}^{2}-2x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{12-2x-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12-2x-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} & =0 \\ 12-2x-2{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+x-6 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-3,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-3$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-3$ and $x=2.$

q-127391:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+n\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0<x<2\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0<x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (0,2\pi )$ are 

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{4},\,x=\frac{5\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (0,2\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (0,2\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{4}=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

q-132567:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ -3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})+n\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{6}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{\pi }{6},\,x=\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{6}=-\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

q-8616:
The counterclockwise angle that the ray makes with the positive $x$-axis is

$$
\pi +\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{6\pi }{5}.
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is $\theta =\frac{6\pi }{5}.$

q-87127:
The counterclockwise angle that the ray makes with the positive $x$-axis is

$$
2\pi -\frac{2\pi }{7}=\frac{12\pi }{7}.
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is $\theta =\frac{12\pi }{7}.$

q-120704:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{6}}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the third quadrant. So, we find the angle in the third quadrant that has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}.
$$

q-41263:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(8,\frac{5\pi }{6}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-4\sqrt{3} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =8\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-4\sqrt{3},4).$

q-69835:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(2+3)-2(1+6)-1(-1+4) \\  & =4\cdot 5-2\cdot 7-1\cdot 3 \\  & =20-14-3 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(T)=3\ne 0$, the matrix is **not** singular. 

Therefore, only statement III is true.

q-84994:
First, note that $(\frac{12}{3})$ means the same thing as ${}_{12}{C}_{3}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=12$ and $r=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{12}{C}_{3} & =\frac{12!}{(12-3)!3!} \\  & =\frac{12!}{9!3!} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10\cdot \cancel{9!}}{\cancel{9!}\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10}{6} \\  & =220.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36905:
A function is invertible if and only if it's a one-to-one function. To determine which of the functions are one-to-one, we use the horizontal line test.

From the above, we see that in each of the four given graphs, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. Therefore, these are not one-to-one functions. As a result, none of them correspond to an invertible function.

q-49234:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=\frac{k\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=2{e}^{{x}_{k}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[2{e}^{(k\operatorname{ln}⁡2)/n}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=2{e}^{x}$ and $b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

q-77543:
To find the image of $A$ under the action of $T$, we first create a column-vector $x$ containing the coordinates of $A:$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $x$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $Tx:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Tx & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The result, $Tx,$ contains the coordinates of ${A}^{′}.$ Therefore, ${A}^{′}(2,1).$
